newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says its diplomacy looks east in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Russia says its diplomacy looks east in 1997.

text.p: Russia, angered by NATO's plans to take in new European members, will step up its diplomatic offensive in Asia in 1997, Interfax news agency quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Grigory Karasin as saying on Friday.
"The coming year will be very intensive for the Asian-Pacific orientation of Russian foreign policy," Karasin told Interfax in an interview.

"It is noteworthy that the Asian orientation offers an example of how to think anew and not to strive towards the creation of new dividing lines, the widening of military blocs etcetera," he said, clearly referring to NATO's expansion plans.
Moscow regards the Atlantic alliance's intention of admitting several former communist countries in central and eastern Europe as a direct threat to its own security.
Karasin hailed warming ties between Russia and China as "a trust-based partnership evolving into strategic cooperation in the next century", Interfax said.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin is expected to visit Moscow in April for a summit that will set the seal on improved relations between the two giant neighbours. China's Prime Minister Li Peng met President Boris Yeltsin and other top officials during a visit to Moscow last week.
Karasin said Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was also likely to visit Moscow in the first half of 1997.

He said Russia's relations with Japan, long hampered by a territorial dispute involving four islands, had benefited from "dynamic realism" in 1996. An inter-governmental commission on economic cooperation will meet in Tokyo in February, he said.

Japan recently announced it was unblocking loans to Russia, frozen because of the territorial row, and signalled it would consider joint development of the islands, which have held up a formal peace treaty between the World War Two foes.
